article:
Some strings are not content

A secret is a key that proves you are allowed to do a dangerous thing: charge a card, write to a repo, send mail, talk to a model as you. If it sits in a public file, it is not a secret. It is a gift to strangers.

Environment variables are how you hand a secret to the running app without putting it in GitHub. On Vercel they live in the project settings. On your laptop they live in a file you do not commit, or in the shell.

The ones this site already uses

EDIT_SECRET is the passphrase you type to tend the tape and edit a lesson. GITHUB_TOKEN is the fine-grained PAT that lets the site commit. They are different strings. Putting the PAT in the prompt box would be a good way to have a bad week.

When you add a variable, rebuild production. The old deploy does not know the new key exists.

How I actually do it

I tell Grok the name of the variable and what it is for. I do not paste the value into the chat if I can help it. I make tokens that can only touch one repo, with the smallest permission that works — Contents, not the keys to the account.

If a key leaks, you do not write a sad paragraph. You revoke it. Then you make another. Then you check the repo history.

Where noobs get stuck

Committing .env because “it works on my machine.” Pasting a Stripe live key into Slack. Using one god-token for every project until the end of time. Or the freeze: being so scared of keys that they never ship anything that needs one.

Film this

Vercel → Settings → Environment Variables. Add a dummy name. Redeploy. Show the app reading it. Then show a repo search for the word TOKEN and a clean result.

Do this before chapter 09

  • Add one env var to the project. Redeploy.
  • Confirm the value is not in any file on GitHub.
  • Write a two-line note: what the key does, where it lives.
  • If you have ever pasted a live key into a chat, rotate it today.
